title: Report on Studying Abroad at the Medical University of Vienna and the National University of Singapore
paragraphs: Using the Nagoya University exchange program, I was allowed to study at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria for two months and at the National University of Singapore in Singapore for one month. I would like to write about each study abroad experience in turn.

- Medical University of Vienna. My clerkship period in Vienna was two months, April to May 2013, during which I rotated for one month each through thoracic surgery and the family doctor (GP: General Practice). I remember that April 2, the first day of the hospital clerkship at the Medical University of Vienna, was very cold and it was snowing. Changing between subway lines I was not yet used to, I arrived at the hospital at 7:30, thirty minutes before the meeting time. The hospital clerkship of the Medical University of Vienna is carried out at the Vienna General Hospital (AKH: Allgemeines Krankenhaus der Stadt Wien). The AKH is a very large hospital, with about 1500 doctors and about 2100 beds. There is no English signage in the hospital, and it is easy to get lost even inside.

Each day in thoracic surgery began with a conference from 7:30, followed by drawing blood on the ward, observing rounds, and then observing surgery. Because there was a Korean doctor, the conference discussions were held in English, but other examinations and communication among doctors were in German. Once the work on the ward, such as blood drawing, was done, I observed surgery. The actual observation had a fairly free atmosphere, and the doctors told me I could go and see any operation I was interested in. What made me feel a difference from Japan was that lung transplant operations were performed frequently, and during the one-month rotation I was able to observe several, for example for pulmonary fibrosis and primary pulmonary hypertension. Particularly impressive was one case of a combined heart-lung transplant in a child, in which a brain-dead donor arose in Budapest, Hungary, and the transplant was done in Vienna. It was a very interesting case both for being a combined heart-lung transplant and for the cross-border provision of organs.

After thoracic surgery, I rotated through the family doctor (GP: General Practice). The content of the clerkship in GP was extremely wide-ranging. It seemed to be a program run by the department of public health, and besides visiting refugee support facilities, AIDS patient support facilities and nursing facilities for the elderly, I was given several opportunities to observe the night-visit emergency medical service and the practice of family doctors inside and outside Vienna. In observing family doctors, I had few opportunities to actually communicate with patients, but I was able to talk with the doctors about medical care in Austria and Japan and spent a very fulfilling time. It became a clerkship that made me think deeply about seeing medical care from the standpoint of society as a whole, not only hospital care.
On weekends, I was able to fully enjoy European culture by going sightseeing in Vienna and travelling to surrounding countries.

- National University of Singapore. After returning to Japan for about a week at the beginning of June, I headed to Singapore. My first impression of Singapore was of a clean and orderly country. There was almost no litter on the roadside, and I felt it was such a clean environment that it was hard to say which was better than Japan.

The clerkship in Singapore was for one month, from June 10 to July 5, at the Singapore General Hospital (SGH: Singapore General Hospital), in neurosurgery. I heard that students of the National University of Singapore train at the National University Hospital (NUH: National University Hospital), the SGH and about ten other hospitals. Among them, the SGH, established in 1821 and with about 1700 beds, is the oldest and largest hospital in Singapore.

On the first day, an orientation was held first at the Dean's office of the National University of Singapore. About ten exchange students who were starting their clerkships that week had gathered there. The countries included the UK, Indonesia, Malaysia, China and Taiwan, and I also heard that there are many exchange students from Germany, Switzerland, France, Australia, Korea, the United States and elsewhere. There we received explanations of the outline, rules and norms of the training hospital, and in the afternoon there was a detailed orientation at the SGH.

Each day in neurosurgery at the SGH followed the flow of a meeting from 8 a.m., observing rounds, and observing surgery. Each student was assigned one Supervisor and one Medical Officer, and the clerkship was one in which we acted according to the instructions of those doctors. The actual content of the clerkship seemed to depend greatly on the doctor in charge, and in my case I was given relatively many opportunities for medical interviews, physical examinations and simple procedures, so I was able to lead a fulfilling clerkship life. As for surgery, it seemed difficult for students to take part, and it was basically observation.

The official languages in Singapore are English, Standard Mandarin, Malay and Tamil. By ethnic group, about 75% are Chinese, about 15% Malay and about 8% Indian, and my actual impression was also that the proportion of Chinese is large, and most of the language heard in the streets was Chinese. Conversations between doctors are in English, but in conversations with patients who cannot speak English, doctors switched between Chinese, Malay and so on according to the patient (beside the patient's bed was written something like Language: English, Mandarin, Malay). On the other hand, for patients who cannot speak English, there was also a situation in which they cannot easily be seen unless there is a doctor who speaks their mother tongue, and I was able to witness part of the problems Singapore faces.

As described above, through my three months of study abroad in Vienna and Singapore, I was able to have many experiences that I could not have in Japan. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 粕谷, who looked after me in this study abroad, the doctors of the International Exchange Office, everyone at the academic affairs office, and the doctors in Vienna and Singapore. Thank you very much indeed.
